doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

chapter: Joe Darensbourg and the Creole question
title: Creole identity and colour gradations
summary: Discussion of what Creole means, Johnny St. Cyr and Darensbourg, British mixture, and King Oliver preferring light-coloured bandsmen.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That Creole question is really quite complex.
Yeah. For sure. From Louisiana through to California, you know. There’s a whole Creole scene still in California.
How they define themselves or how other people define them.

Well you know Johnny St. Cyr was a Creole and he was as black as the ace of spades wasn’t he? Joe would look Hispanic to you if he were here today. He was a Creole. A Creole, officially, as I understand it, is a mixture of French, Spanish and black. And he was never unhappy about that. That was a perfectly fair description for him. His brothers and sisters did not wish that to be — the description that they wanted to hear or to see in print.
Is there anything in England that’s analogous to that?

Well we of course, we are now more and more of a mixture in England, aren’t we? We have a tremendous number of Afro-Caribbeans in Britain and of course black African, black American, black British of West African descent, Nigerians and the like, a lot of Asians, so there is a some degree of intermixing. And you are still aware of the fact that gradations of color are considered important. Lighter is better than darker, which I understand was the case here also in the early days. King Oliver wouldn’t employ guys who were really dark.

Oh no. He was very dark, but he didn’t want anyone else in the band that was very dark because the perception was that that was somehow socially less good. A light colored band looked more acceptable.
More likely to get work perhaps.
It’s a funny world you know. I remember the first time I saw a black person on television speaking with a very strong English accent, it just seemed very strange.
Well we’ve all got these sort of perceptions, haven’t we?
